vignette:
He is a 75-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as careful, polished, and self-contained, the kind of person who has spent much of his life managing risk by staying composed. For years, his work as a cybersecurity analyst has matched that part of him: he is used to scanning for threats, tracing weak points, and responding quickly when something goes wrong. He has built a life around vigilance and control. Before the trauma, he was also a widower who kept a steady routine, lived modestly, and took quiet pride in being dependable, especially for his family.

The traumatic period begins when his adult child becomes critically ill. At first, he tries to approach the situation the way he would approach a breach at work: gather information, keep notes, anticipate the next step. He learns every detail about diagnoses, medications, test results, and timelines. He sits in hospital rooms with a laptop balanced on his knees, answering work messages between consultations, because staying busy feels safer than allowing himself to feel the terror rising in his chest. He tells himself that if he can remain useful, if he can track the data accurately enough, he can help protect his child. He sleeps in fragments and eats little, but for a while he keeps functioning.

As the illness becomes life-threatening, his confidence in his ability to control outcomes collapses. He remembers the first moment a physician's face changes before speaking, the pause that tells him something is very wrong. After that, time seems to split into alarms, fluorescent hospital light, and the constant waiting for updates. He sits through long nights in the intensive care unit listening to machines breathe for his child. He does not cry in front of others. Instead, he becomes inwardly rigid, with a sense that any lapse in attention could cost his child's life. He checks and rechecks information compulsively, rereads medical emails, and calls the hospital more than he thinks is reasonable, unable to tolerate uncertainty. His mind begins to race with images of what could happen, and he feels trapped in a state of alert that never turns off.

When his child survives, the relief is real but incomplete. He expects the fear to lift, but instead it stays lodged in his body. He finds that his mind returns to the hospital in flashes: the sound of monitors, the look on his child's face, the worst conversations he has ever had. He avoids talking about that period and changes the subject when relatives ask how he coped. He keeps his distance from the hospital route in town and feels a sharp tightening in his chest when he sees medical equipment on television. At night, he wakes suddenly with the sensation that something terrible is happening again. He checks his phone for messages, then checks again, even when there is nothing new. Sleep becomes shallow and broken, and mornings feel like he has already been fighting for hours.

At work, his concentration falters in ways that embarrass him. He rereads reports, loses track of passwords, and finds himself staring at code without taking it in. Because he is nearing the end of his career, he feels ashamed that his mind is not as steady as it once was. He notices that his tolerance for error has vanished. Small problems in his job can trigger a disproportionate surge of irritation or panic, as if every warning signal now carries the weight of the hospital crisis. He remains highly functional on the surface, but it costs him more energy than anyone sees.

He is also changed in his relationships. Since becoming widowed, he had already learned to live with loneliness, but this trauma makes him more isolated. He loves his surviving family deeply, yet he holds them at a slight distance, afraid of how much he can lose. He wants reassurance and resists asking for it. He can speak calmly about dates, appointments, and practical matters, but when the conversation turns to feelings, he becomes quiet and guarded. At times he is overwhelmed by guilt, wondering if he missed signs, if he should have pushed harder, if there was something he did or failed to do that made the ordeal worse. The guilt does not resolve into a clear thought; it lingers as a heavy, private burden.

Even now, he lives with a sense that danger can return without warning. He remains watchful in a way that is exhausting rather than protective. He has become a man who continues to scan for threats long after the crisis has passed, as though his body has not yet received the message that his child is no longer in immediate danger.
